title: Autoimmune Liver Disease: AIH Types and Scores, PBC Criteria, PSC Imaging
summary: Separate autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis by target, antibody and diagnostic rule: AIH antibody types and IAIHG scores, the PBC two-of-three criteria and why AMA titre does not track severity, and why PSC is diagnosed by cholangiography.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 55 Hits 8 (AIH types and scores), 11 (PBC 2 of 3) and 12 (PSC), and Trap 2 (AMA titre and severity), checked against APASL AIH 2021 and PBC 2022 guidance, Terziroli Beretta-Piccoli 2022, the BSG/UK-PSC 2019 and Japanese 2017 PSC guidelines, Palmela 2018 and Jhaveri 2017. The Clin Liver Dis summary of the AASLD 2018 PBC guidance is listed but could not be re-opened on fact-check (PMC reCAPTCHA), so it verifies nothing. Qualified: the APASL 2022 PBC criteria do not fix the ALP ≥1.5× ULN for >24 weeks or AMA ≥1:40 thresholds (register flag rv-pbc-criteria-thresholds); PSC ALP can be normal, against the reviewer’s “3–10× ULN in 95%” (rv-psc-alp-range); reported p-ANCA frequency in PSC is lower and wider than 65–95% (rv-psc-panca-frequency). Not taught: AIH minimal titres in children, treatment, overlap-syndrome criteria in detail.

objectives: Distinguish AIH, PBC and PSC by target, laboratory pattern and key test.
Name the antibodies of type 1 and type 2 AIH and the cut-offs of the simplified and revised IAIHG scores.
Apply the PBC two-of-three rule and explain why AMA titre is not a severity marker.
Explain why PSC is diagnosed by cholangiography and why a normal ALP does not exclude it.

scenes.title: Three livers, three attackers
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients with abnormal liver tests. (1) A 52-year-old woman with itching and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP and GGT), AMA positive; (2) a 13-year-old girl with hepatitis (high ALT), raised IgG, anti-LKM-1 positive; (3) a 30-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and a cholestatic pattern, AMA negative. Question token: “Which autoimmune liver disease — and which test proves it?”

cues.text: Three invented patients with abnormal liver tests: a fifty-two-year-old woman with itching, cholestasis and a positive AMA; a thirteen-year-old girl with hepatitis and anti-LKM-1.
And a thirty-year-old man with ulcerative colitis, cholestasis and a negative AMA.
Which autoimmune liver disease does each have, and which test actually settles it?

scenes.title: Three targets in one liver
scenes.altText: Schematic: a liver lobule with hepatocytes, small intrahepatic bile ducts and large bile ducts. Three cards. Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH): attack on hepatocytes — hepatitis pattern, raised IgG, interface hepatitis, circulating autoantibodies. Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): small interlobular bile ducts — nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis, cholestatic pattern, AMA. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC): intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic ducts — multifocal strictures, cholestatic pattern, strong link with inflammatory bowel disease; no reliable autoantibody.

cues.text: The three classic autoimmune liver diseases aim at different targets. Autoimmune hepatitis attacks the liver cells themselves: a hepatitis pattern, raised IgG, interface hepatitis on biopsy, and circulating autoantibodies.
Primary biliary cholangitis destroys the small bile ducts inside the liver, a non-suppurative destructive cholangitis, so the pattern is cholestatic and the antibody is anti-mitochondrial.
Classic primary sclerosing cholangitis scars the larger ducts, inside and outside the liver, into many short strictures. It travels with inflammatory bowel disease.
The British guideline is blunt: no reliable autoantibody has been identified for it.

scenes.title: AIH: antibody types and scores
scenes.altText: Type card: AIH type 1 = ANA and/or anti-smooth muscle antibody (SMA), about 90% of cases, children and adults. AIH type 2 = anti-LKM-1 (target cytochrome P450 2D6) and/or anti-LC-1; mainly a paediatric disease. Anti-SLA is the only AIH-specific antibody; it occurs in both types but is detected in only 20–30% of patients by commercial solid-phase assays. Caveat: anti-LKM-1 is found in up to 13% of chronic hepatitis C, so exclude HCV. Score card: IAIHG simplified criteria (2008) — autoantibodies (ANA or SMA ≥1:40 = 1 point, ≥1:80 = 2; anti-LKM-1 ≥1:40 or anti-SLA = 2; maximum 2), IgG, histology, absence of viral hepatitis; ≥6 probable, ≥7 definite. Revised original score, pretreatment: >15 definite, 10–15 probable (posttreatment >17 definite, 12–17 probable).

cues.text: Autoimmune hepatitis is typed by its antibodies. Type one, about ninety percent of cases, carries antinuclear and or anti-smooth muscle antibody, in children and adults.

Type two carries anti-LKM-1, whose target is cytochrome P450 2D6, and or anti-liver cytosol type 1. It is mainly a disease of children. Anti-LKM-1 also turns up in some chronic hepatitis C, so hepatitis C must be excluded.

No single antibody is diagnostic, so the international group scores the case. The simplified score adds points for autoantibody titre, IgG, histology and absence of viral hepatitis: six is probable, seven or more definite.
The older revised score includes many more items. Before treatment, more than fifteen points is definite and ten to fifteen probable.

props.title: Simplified score
lines: Ab titre · IgG · histology · no viral

scenes.title: PBC two of three, PSC by picture
scenes.altText: PBC card (APASL 2022): diagnosis when 2 of 3 are met — biochemical cholestasis (raised ALP, with imaging excluding obstruction); AMA, or PBC-specific ANA (anti-sp100, anti-gp210) if AMA negative; histology of nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis of interlobular ducts. Some reviews give thresholds (ALP ≥1.5× ULN for >24 weeks; AMA ≥1:40). AMA alone is not enough: AMA-positive patients with normal liver tests are followed. About 5% of PBC is AMA-negative. PSC card: cholangiography (MRCP, or ERCP) showing short multifocal strictures with a beaded appearance; onion-skin periductal fibrosis is the histological hallmark but often absent on small biopsies; IBD in about 70% (60–80% in Western surveys), mostly ulcerative colitis; ALP may be normal (17% at diagnosis in one Japanese survey). Hook answers.

cues.text: Primary biliary cholangitis needs two of three: cholestatic biochemistry with raised ALP and no duct obstruction on imaging; AMA, or the PBC-specific sp100 or gp210 antibodies; and destructive cholangitis on histology.
An AMA alone is not a diagnosis. With normal liver tests, the guideline advises yearly follow-up, not a label.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is diagnosed by imaging: MRCP shows short strictures alternating with slightly dilated segments, a beaded duct. Onion-skin fibrosis is the biopsy hallmark, but small biopsies often miss it. ALP can even be normal.

Back to the hook. The woman fits primary biliary cholangitis. The girl fits type two autoimmune hepatitis once hepatitis C is excluded. The man with colitis needs a cholangiogram for primary sclerosing cholangitis.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A rising AMA titre means PBC is worsening” (✓ AMA level does not reflect PBC severity; it is diagnostic, not a monitoring tool); “Anti-LKM-1 positive = type 2 AIH” (✓ found in up to 13% of chronic hepatitis C; exclude HCV and score the case); “Normal ALP rules out PSC” (✓ ALP can be normal; cholangiography decides).

cues.text: Trap one: a rising AMA titre means the disease is worsening. No: the AMA level does not reflect severity. It diagnoses; it does not monitor.
Trap two: anti-LKM-1 proves type two autoimmune hepatitis. No: it appears in some chronic hepatitis C. Exclude the virus and score the case.
Trap three: a normal ALP rules out sclerosing cholangitis. No: ALP can be normal, and the cholangiogram decides.

scenes.title: Cells, small pipes, big pipes
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “AIH eats the CELLS (antibodies plus a score), PBC blocks the SMALL PIPES (two of three, AMA), PSC kinks the BIG PIPES (a beaded picture, not an antibody).” Tokens: cells = AIH · small pipes = PBC · big pipes = PSC. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: autoimmune hepatitis eats the cells and is scored from antibodies; primary biliary cholangitis blocks the small pipes and is two of three with AMA; primary sclerosing cholangitis kinks the big pipes and is a beaded picture, not an antibody.
Where it breaks: the diseases overlap, such as PBC with AIH features or AIH with sclerosing cholangitis; small-duct PSC has a normal cholangiogram; and about five percent of PBC is AMA-negative.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “AIH = antibody type + score · PBC = 2 of 3, AMA does not track severity”, “PSC = beaded cholangiogram, not an antibody”.

cues.text: Diagnose autoimmune hepatitis by antibody type plus a score, primary biliary cholangitis by two of three criteria with an AMA titre that does not track severity, and primary sclerosing cholangitis by a beaded cholangiogram rather than an antibody.

props.label: AIH = antibody type + score · PBC = 2 of 3, AMA ≠ severity
PSC = beaded cholangiogram, not an antibody

explanation.what: Plain language: in autoimmune liver disease the immune system attacks either the liver cells (autoimmune hepatitis) or the bile ducts, small ones (primary biliary cholangitis) or large ones (primary sclerosing cholangitis). Antibodies help, but each disease has its own rule for diagnosis. Scientific terms: antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibody (SMA), anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 (anti-LKM-1; CYP2D6), anti-liver cytosol type 1 (anti-LC-1), anti-soluble liver antigen (anti-SLA), International Autoimmune Hepatitis Group (IAIHG) simplified and revised scores, antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), anti-sp100, anti-gp210, nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), onion-skin periductal fibrosis, p-ANCA.
explanation.why: None of these antibodies is fully disease-specific (anti-LKM-1 occurs in chronic hepatitis C; AMA can be positive with normal liver tests), and PSC has no reliable antibody, so diagnosis combines serology with biochemistry, histology, imaging and exclusion of other causes.
explanation.measure: AIH type 1: ANA and/or SMA (about 90% of cases); type 2: anti-LKM-1 and/or anti-LC-1, mainly paediatric. Simplified score ≥6 probable, ≥7 definite; revised pretreatment >15 definite, 10–15 probable (posttreatment >17 definite, 12–17 probable). PBC: 2 of 3 (cholestasis with raised ALP; AMA or sp100/gp210; destructive cholangitis on histology); AMA level does not reflect severity; about 5% AMA-negative. PSC: beaded multifocal strictures on MRCP/ERCP; onion-skin fibrosis often absent on small biopsies; IBD in about 70%, mostly ulcerative colitis; ALP may be normal.
explanation.differs: Hepatocyte (AIH) vs small intrahepatic duct (PBC) vs large intra- and extrahepatic duct (PSC); hepatitis vs cholestatic pattern; antibody-and-score (AIH) vs two-of-three (PBC) vs imaging (PSC).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the antibody of type 1 or type 2 AIH, pick the diagnosis from a two-of-three PBC vignette, recognise PSC from a beaded cholangiogram in a patient with ulcerative colitis, or reject AMA titre as a monitoring test.

right.label: PSC
points: No reliable antibody; IBD in about 70%

mnemonic.text: AIH eats the CELLS (antibodies plus a score), PBC blocks the SMALL PIPES (two of three, AMA), PSC kinks the BIG PIPES (a beaded picture, not an antibody).
mnemonic.explanation: Links each disease to its target and its diagnostic rule.
mnemonic.limitation: Overlap syndromes exist (PBC with AIH features, AIH with sclerosing cholangitis); small-duct PSC has a normal cholangiogram; about 5% of PBC is AMA-negative.

analogyLimitations: Frequencies vary between populations and studies.
takeaway: Diagnose autoimmune hepatitis by antibody type plus a score, primary biliary cholangitis by two of three criteria with an AMA titre that does not track severity, and primary sclerosing cholangitis by a beaded cholangiogram rather than an antibody.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has hepatitis, raised IgG and a positive anti-LKM-1; hepatitis C testing is negative. Which antigen does anti-LKM-1 recognise, and which AIH type does it define?

options.rationale: Correct. Anti-LKM-1 targets CYP2D6 and, with or without anti-LC-1, defines type 2 AIH, mainly a paediatric disease.
Incorrect. PDC-E2 is the main AMA antigen of PBC, and type 1 AIH is defined by ANA and/or SMA.
Incorrect. Actin is a target of anti-smooth muscle antibody, a type 1 AIH marker.
Incorrect. This is the anti-LC-1 antigen, and anti-LC-1 is a type 2 marker.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a raised ALP and GGT, no duct dilatation on ultrasound, and a positive AMA. A year later her AMA titre has doubled while her ALP is unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: She meets two of three PBC criteria; the AMA rise does not indicate worsening disease
options.rationale: Correct. Cholestatic biochemistry plus AMA meets the two-of-three rule, and the AMA level does not reflect PBC severity.

options.text: The doubled AMA titre shows progression and needs treatment escalation
options.rationale: Incorrect. AMA level does not reflect disease severity and is not a monitoring tool.

options.text: PBC cannot be diagnosed without a liver biopsy
options.rationale: Incorrect. Histology is only one of the three criteria; two are enough.

options.text: A positive AMA alone would have been enough even with normal liver tests
options.rationale: Incorrect. AMA reactivity alone is not sufficient; AMA-positive patients with normal liver tests are followed up.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has a cholestatic liver profile and a negative AMA. Which finding best supports primary sclerosing cholangitis?

options.text: MRCP showing short multifocal strictures with a beaded appearance
options.rationale: Correct. Cholangiography showing multifocal strictures and beading is the main diagnostic evidence for PSC.
Incorrect. p-ANCA is reported in a variable proportion of PSC and also in ulcerative colitis and AIH; no reliable autoantibody confirms PSC.
Incorrect. A normal ALP does not exclude PSC, but it does not support it either.
Incorrect. Anti-sp100 is a PBC-specific antinuclear antibody.

claims.text: AIH targets hepatocytes, PBC small interlobular ducts, PSC intra- and/or extrahepatic ducts; PSC has no reliable autoantibody.
AIH type 1 = ANA and/or SMA (about 90%); type 2 = anti-LKM-1 (CYP2D6) and/or anti-LC-1, mainly paediatric; anti-LKM-1 in some chronic hepatitis C.
Simplified IAIHG score ≥6 probable, ≥7 definite; revised pretreatment >15 definite, 10–15 probable.
PBC two-of-three criteria; AMA level does not reflect severity; AMA alone not sufficient; about 5% AMA-negative.
PSC diagnosed by cholangiography (beading); onion-skin fibrosis often missed on biopsy; IBD in about 70%, mostly ulcerative colitis; ALP may be normal; p-ANCA variable and nonspecific.
Reviewer: type 2 AIH is more aggressive; AIH minimal titres in children (1:10 LKM-1, 1:20 ANA).
claims.note: Not taught; the sources read describe an aggressive historical anti-LKM cohort but no direct comparison was read.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 55 Hit 11 gives fixed PBC thresholds (ALP ≥1.5× ULN for >24 weeks; AMA ≥1:40; florid duct lesion). The APASL 2022 guidance states the two-of-three rule without these thresholds or a duration and accepts the PBC-specific anti-sp100/anti-gp210; the fixed thresholds appear in some reviews (for example Jhaveri 2017). The lesson teaches the current wording (register flag rv-pbc-criteria-thresholds).

Ch. 55 Hit 12 states ALP is 3–10× ULN in 95% of PSC. BSG 2019 reports abnormal liver biochemistry in about 75%, and a Japanese survey found 17.1% with ALP not above ULN at diagnosis; the lesson teaches that ALP may be normal (register flag rv-psc-alp-range).

Ch. 55 Hit 12 gives p-ANCA in 65–95% of PSC. Palmela 2018 reports 26–85% and the Japanese guideline 50–80%; BSG 2019 states no reliable autoantibodies exist. The lesson does not teach a single frequency (register flag rv-psc-panca-frequency).

morphology.note: No micrographs or cholangiograms; diseases shown as cards.

verification.notes: 5 factual claims checked against APASL AIH 2021 and PBC 2022, Terziroli Beretta-Piccoli 2022, BSG/UK-PSC 2019, the Japanese PSC guideline 2017, Palmela 2018 and Jhaveri 2017 (the AASLD 2018 summary could not be re-opened on fact-check and verifies nothing); 1 pending (type 2 AIH aggressiveness; paediatric titres).
